headline: AI data centre spend in Australia has limited domestic inflation impact, with most equipment and chips imported
reasoning: Justin Fabo notes that while there is growing data centre investment in Australia, much of the equipment, chips and key components are imported rather than domestically sourced. As a result, the domestic economic and inflation impact has been modest. There is some marginal benefit for employment in engineering and non-residential construction, but it is not expected to be a significant driver of the Australian economy over the next couple of years.
quote: Even though some of that the the building and the people needed to to build those data centres is obviously domestically sourced, a lot of it, particularly the equipment and the chips and the stuff that goes into the data centres is imported. So the impact on the domestic economy, um, has not been massive so far, and we don't anticipate will be a massive thing over the next couple of years.
episode_title: AI puts markets to the test ahead of key central bank decisions

headline: Australian housing market investor activity briefly pulled back on tax noise but is stabilising, while higher mortgage rates remain a headwind
reasoning: Fabo references Ray White data suggesting a drop in investor activity around the federal budget due to uncertainty around housing taxation, followed by a partial recovery as the dust settled. He characterises this as a typical overreaction and subsequent normalisation. However, he notes that mortgage rates have risen, making established housing more expensive to purchase, which is an ongoing structural headwind for the market regardless of near-term sentiment shifts.
quote: At least since the budget, and it's not just since then actually it's been longer, but we have seen a drop off on their numbers in the share of investor activity in terms of what they see through their network. But in recent weeks it has improved again, to be kind of back close to where it was at the budget. So that's not that surprising. You know, when there's a lot of noise around taxation around housing, the vested interests and potential investors just kind of pull back a little bit to see where it lands and typically to overreact. And then things kind of settle down. It feels like at the moment we're in that period where things are just settling down a bit and we're getting a clearer picture on the housing market. But what hasn't changed is that interest rates have gone back up, including mortgage rates. Makes it more expensive to buy established housing.
episode_title: AI puts markets to the test ahead of key central bank decisions

headline: Global AI and data centre spend is pushing up semiconductor and memory prices, adding to goods inflation globally including in Australia
reasoning: Fabo argues the more significant inflation channel from AI spending is global rather than local. There is excess demand for memory and semiconductors, which are used not just in data centres but also in consumer goods and cars. Prices of these components are rising sharply, contributing to goods price inflation in both the US and Australia after several years of falling or flat durable goods prices.
quote: The way to think about that from an inflation perspective is more, um, the global impact of AI spend, not the local impact of AI spend. So we know at the global level there's a huge squeeze going on where there's excess demand for memory, there's excess demand for semiconductor chips. The prices of those things which aren't just used for data centers, they go into a lot of consumer goods and cars. The prices of those things are going through the roof. So it's more a global picture that it's having from this data center and memory and semiconductor spend that's having an impact on inflation for some goods. You're seeing that in the US inflation numbers. You're seeing it a little bit in the Australian numbers where we had a number of years where goods prices, particularly durable goods were falling in price or at worse flat. That is not the case now.
episode_title: AI puts markets to the test ahead of key central bank decisions

headline: Australian Q2 trimmed mean inflation expected to print 0.9–1%, still too high relative to RBA's 2–3% target
reasoning: Fabo notes that Australia's inflation is already above the 2–3% target band and the upcoming June quarter CPI is the key focus for the RBA given the monthly series is still relatively new. The RBA's own May forecasts pointed to trimmed mean inflation of 0.9–1% for the quarter, which Fabo's team also expects. While this may not surprise to the upside, it is still a very strong underlying inflation print, keeping the RBA focused on inflation risks even as the real economy shows signs of slowing.
quote: For Australia our inflation is already too high. I think everyone knows that we have a target of 2 to 3%. The numbers we get out this week are not just for the June month, but for the June quarter, which is still, by and large, the main focus for the RBA because the monthly series is still quite new. So the key focus will be on the key underlying measure that they look at is so-called trim mean inflation. It's very important. They are expecting a reasonably strong number of between 0.9 and 1% based on their forecasts back in May. That's exactly where we think when we have a lot more information now where we think the number will come out. So maybe not a surprise to the upside, but nonetheless, still we expect a very strong inflation print for the quarter in an underlying sense.
episode_title: AI puts markets to the test ahead of key central bank decisions

headline: Justin Fabo sees Australian housing in early stages of a modest, normal correction — not a calamitous decline — supported by strong population growth and tight rental markets.
reasoning: Fabo notes that housing prices are falling in most capital cities except Perth following the rise in interest rates, including mortgage rates, which has reduced activity from owner-occupiers, first home buyers and investors. He characterises this as a normal, modest correction rather than a calamitous decline, pointing to historical precedent where housing prices do periodically fall in nominal and real terms. He argues the underlying bid for housing remains intact due to strong population growth, tight rental markets and very few homeowners in negative equity. Unemployment is still low, and while sentiment has turned negative and buyers are sitting on the sidelines, he views that as reasonably healthy. He suggests it is better to have a modest correction now than to allow prices to run another 20–30%, which would be unhealthy.
quote: It feels like we're at the early stages of that process, but we we aren't in the camp where we're thinking that this is going to be a calamitous decline in housing prices. And the main reason for that is that we still have strong population growth, strong underlying demand for housing, tight rental markets, um, so that that bid for housing is still there beneath the surface. I think people will just sit on the sidelines at the moment to just to see how things play out. That's actually reasonably healthy... it is not a disastrous situation that the media or parts of the media like to play out. And it's better that it happens now when we get, you know, hopefully kind of a modest correction and some rationality going back into these markets. Um, before it just went another, you know, 20 or 30%, that would have been very unhealthy.
episode_title: AI puts markets to the test ahead of key central bank decisions

headline: Australian housing price declines are historically common and not unusual, with Sydney and Melbourne most cyclical
reasoning: Justin Fabo notes that falls in housing prices are not unusual and are actually quite common historically, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, where there have been multiple declines over the past decade. He argues that much of the media noise around house price falls is amplified by the media cycle. Nationally, price declines are less frequent because the various markets average out. He cautions against attempting to forecast the magnitude of falls. Prices are still rising in some regional areas and Perth even as Sydney and Melbourne decline.
quote: I mean, as you say, prices are falling kind of at the national level. But we know there's there's not one housing market in Australia, so prices aren't falling everywhere. But the larger prices are price declines in Sydney and Melbourne. Um, we've kind of seen that um, in the past. Um, so prices are still rising in some other places, particularly regional Australia, where a lot of people live in Perth as well. We typically don't kind of play this game, I call it, where people like to, you know, get um, and come up with the biggest number for the fall in house prices. Um, because invariably you kind of get it wrong. Um, but it is the case that when you look, um, historically that falls in housing prices are not unusual. Um, they're actually quite common.
episode_title: Beyond falling house prices - the economic ripple effect

headline: Falling Australian house prices will weigh on private demand via reduced housing turnover, durable goods spending and stamp duty revenue
reasoning: Fabo's key macro concern is not the wealth effect per se but rather the behavioural changes that accompany weak housing prices. When prices fall, housing turnover drops sharply, which flows through to reduced spending on durables and household goods, lower stamp duty revenues, and less activity for real estate agents. He highlights a historical high correlation between real housing price growth and private demand — consumption and housing construction — suggesting a period of falling real house prices will likely weigh on the broader economy. The main uncertainty is the magnitude of this effect.
quote: The bigger effect is more through uncertainty and the behavioral changes around changes in housing. Turnover, though turnover falls quite sharply as it is at the moment when when prices are weak, and that that means there's flow on effect and that people are buying less stuff to put in their houses. People move less, but they're buying less durable, for example. So that's where the bigger impact is. There's less money going through stamp duty. You know, real estate agents have less activity. So it's less economic activity. Um, I think that part you just showed was the kind of the key one for me, like cutting through all the noise. If you look over time, there's a high correlation between real housing price growth and what we call private demand in the economy. So private demand is consumption growth by household and housing construction and other types of investment. These things typically swing in terms of growth with with the housing price cycle. So if we're going through a period at the moment where we are, where real housing prices are falling and will fall further. Um, that will likely weigh on private demand growth in your economy.
episode_title: Beyond falling house prices - the economic ripple effect

headline: Negative equity risk from Australian house price falls is limited given the scale of prior nominal price gains
reasoning: Fabo argues that the risk of widespread negative equity is overstated. The large nominal rise in house prices in recent years and the fact that most buyers do not take out 95-100% mortgages means very few households will fall into negative equity even if prices decline a further 10-15%. He acknowledges a small number of recent buyers may already be in negative equity but characterises the aggregate risk as very small and not a major macroeconomic issue.
quote: On this negative equity question, um, you know again that make good headline. Um, but you know, the the rebirth out of the RBA in recent years, but also just the sheer magnitude of the nominal rise in housing prices in recent years means that, you know, there are very few people who will already be in negative equity with, you know, the value of the house is less than your mortgage. And part of that, too, is that most people don't take out 100% mortgages or 95% more mortgages, but there will be a small number who may have entered negative equity. But if prices even fall another 10 to 15%, the share of households in negative equity will be very small. So that's not really a big issue.
episode_title: Beyond falling house prices - the economic ripple effect
